title: Seaborn Cheatsheet
name: Seaborn Cheatsheet
description: High-density syntax recall for Seaborn 0.13.2 focused on common engineering workflows, modern APIs, and copy-paste-ready plotting patterns.

entries.trigger: You need a stable, documented Seaborn install.
entries.snippet:
# pip install seaborn
# conda install seaborn -c conda-forge
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
entries.minimal_notes: Use the pinned stable release line for consistency. Seaborn 0.13.2 is the documented stable version used here.
entries.common_bug: Mixing seaborn versions across notebooks and deployment.

entries.problem: Start a plotting session with a consistent theme.
entries.trigger: You want all plots to share the same visual style.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook", palette="deep")
entries.minimal_notes: Set the theme once near the top of the script or notebook. This helps keep dashboards and reports visually consistent.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that theme settings affect global Matplotlib state.

entries.trigger: You need a built-in dataset for a prototype or demo.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins")
print(df.head())
entries.minimal_notes: Built-in datasets are useful for examples, but they are not a production data source.
entries.common_bug: Using example datasets in a runtime path that must work offline.

entries.trigger: You want a clean default style or presentation style.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
sns.set_theme(style="darkgrid")
sns.set_theme(style="white")
sns.set_theme(style="dark")
sns.set_theme(style="ticks")
entries.minimal_notes: Choose the theme that matches the amount of grid guidance you want. `whitegrid` is often the default for analytical charts.
entries.common_bug: Using `darkgrid` when the plot is already dense and busy.

entries.problem: Adjust scaling for talk, paper, or notebook output.
entries.trigger: Figure elements need to be larger or smaller without manual resizing everywhere.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_context("paper")
sns.set_context("notebook")
sns.set_context("talk")
sns.set_context("poster")
entries.minimal_notes: Use context to scale text and line widths as a group. It is faster than tuning each element individually.
entries.common_bug: Enlarging the figure but forgetting to scale label sizes.

entries.problem: Apply a palette for categorical plots.
entries.trigger: You want readable, consistent series colors.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_palette("deep")
sns.set_palette("muted")
sns.set_palette("pastel")
sns.set_palette("bright")
sns.set_palette("dark")
sns.set_palette("colorblind")
entries.minimal_notes: Use `colorblind` when accessibility matters. Use categorical palettes for discrete groups.
entries.common_bug: Using a continuous palette for discrete categories.

entries.problem: Build a palette for continuous data.
entries.trigger: You need a gradient for counts, densities, or heatmaps.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

palettes = ["viridis", "magma", "rocket", "flare", "crest"]
cmap = sns.color_palette("viridis", as_cmap=True)
entries.minimal_notes: Sequential colormaps are usually better for ordered numeric values. Use a perceptually uniform palette when possible.
entries.common_bug: Picking a rainbow-like gradient for ordered data.

entries.problem: Create a basic scatter plot from a DataFrame.
entries.trigger: You want to inspect a numeric relationship quickly.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use this when raw point positions matter. For dense data, add transparency or sample first.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to drop NaNs in the columns used for axes.

entries.trigger: You want subgroup comparison in one figure.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `hue` is the fastest way to compare classes on the same axes. Keep the legend readable.
entries.common_bug: Mapping the wrong column to `hue` and losing the intended grouping.

entries.trigger: You need one plot with color, size, and marker variation.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.scatterplot(
    data=df,
    x="bill_length_mm",
    y="bill_depth_mm",
    hue="species",
    size="body_mass_g",
    style="island",
    alpha=0.8
)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `size` and `style` only when they add real signal. Too many semantics can make the plot hard to read.
entries.common_bug: Overloading one plot with too many visual encodings.

entries.problem: Plot connected trends across ordered values.
entries.trigger: You need a line chart for time or ordered x values.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("flights")
sns.lineplot(data=df, x="year", y="passengers")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Seaborn aggregates repeated x values by default in many line workflows. Use it for trend detection, not raw point auditing.
entries.common_bug: Expecting a line plot to show every individual observation exactly.

entries.problem: Compare multiple time series on one axis.
entries.trigger: You need one line per group.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("fmri").dropna()
sns.lineplot(data=df, x="timepoint", y="signal", hue="region", style="event")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Combine `hue` and `style` for readable multi-series trends. Keep the number of groups modest.
entries.common_bug: Too many lines with similar colors and no clear ordering.

entries.trigger: You need to inspect the shape of one numeric column.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.histplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", bins=20)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Histogram bin choice matters. Tune `bins` or `binwidth` when the default hides structure.
entries.common_bug: Using too few bins and flattening the distribution.

entries.problem: Add a KDE curve to a histogram.
entries.trigger: You want a smooth density view with the counts.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.histplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", bins=20, kde=True)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: This is useful for quick shape checks. Make sure the density overlay does not hide extremes.
entries.common_bug: Reading the KDE as if it were raw counts.

entries.trigger: You need smooth density comparison across groups.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.kdeplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", hue="species", fill=True, common_norm=False, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `common_norm=False` keeps group shapes easier to compare. Filled KDEs work best with a small number of groups.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that normalization can hide group scale differences.

entries.trigger: You want percentile-style comparison instead of bins.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.ecdfplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", hue="species")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: ECDFs are good when exact ordering matters. They avoid bin-selection issues entirely.
entries.common_bug: Using ECDF when the audience expects counts per bin.

entries.problem: Add a rug for small-sample inspection.
entries.trigger: You want to show the exact observation locations.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.histplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", bins=20)
sns.rugplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", color="black", alpha=0.2)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Rug marks help when sample size is small or exact values matter. Avoid them on very dense data.
entries.common_bug: Cluttering the axis with rugs on large datasets.

entries.trigger: You need a simple aggregated comparison by category.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.barplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex", errorbar="ci")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `barplot` is for summaries, not raw values. Choose the estimator and error bars intentionally.
entries.common_bug: Treating the bar height as a single raw observation.

entries.trigger: You want category frequency instead of a numeric summary.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.countplot(data=df, x="day", hue="sex")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `countplot` is the fastest way to inspect class balance. It is especially useful before modeling.
entries.common_bug: Using a count plot when the x axis is already continuous.

entries.problem: Show category distributions with a box plot.
entries.trigger: You need median, quartiles, and outlier visibility.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Box plots are compact and good for side-by-side comparison. They work well when you need robust summary structure.
entries.common_bug: Expecting a box plot to reveal multimodality clearly.

entries.problem: Show category distributions with a violin plot.
entries.trigger: You want shape information in addition to quartiles.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.violinplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex", cut=0)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `cut=0` to avoid extending beyond the observed range. Violin plots are useful when distribution shape matters.
entries.common_bug: Interpreting smoothed tails as observed data.

entries.problem: Show distribution details for larger datasets.
entries.trigger: You need finer quantiles than a box plot provides.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.boxenplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Boxen plots are helpful when sample size is large. They expose more distribution detail than a standard box plot.
entries.common_bug: Using boxen plots on tiny samples where the extra detail is unstable.

entries.trigger: You need to inspect spread and overlap directly.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.stripplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex", dodge=True, alpha=0.5)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `stripplot` is good for seeing actual points. Jitter or dodge helps reduce overlap.
entries.common_bug: Overplotting hides repeated values and dense regions.

entries.trigger: You want point visibility without overlap.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.swarmplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex", dodge=True, size=3)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use swarm plots when category sizes are small to moderate. They become slow on large datasets.
entries.common_bug: Using swarm plots on large datasets and getting heavy overlap or slow rendering.

entries.trigger: You want a point estimate by category.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.pointplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex", errorbar="ci")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Point plots are compact for trend-like category comparisons. They are useful in dashboards with limited space.
entries.common_bug: Reading line connections as a real continuous trend when categories are unordered.

entries.trigger: You need a fast view of feature relationships.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
num = df.select_dtypes("number")
corr = num.corr(numeric_only=True)
sns.heatmap(corr, cmap="vlag", center=0)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Correlation heatmaps are a standard EDA starting point. Use a diverging palette centered at zero.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to filter to numeric columns before calling `corr()`.

entries.trigger: You want exact values visible in a small matrix.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
corr = df.select_dtypes("number").corr(numeric_only=True)
sns.heatmap(corr, cmap="vlag", center=0, annot=True, fmt=".2f")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use annotations only for small matrices. Dense labels quickly become unreadable.
entries.common_bug: Annotating a large matrix and creating label clutter.

entries.problem: Cluster rows and columns by similarity.
entries.trigger: You want structure in a matrix, not just raw values.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
data = df.select_dtypes("number").corr(numeric_only=True)
sns.clustermap(data, cmap="vlag", center=0, figsize=(6, 6))
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `clustermap` is useful for discovering groups of related variables. It creates its own figure-level layout.
entries.common_bug: Passing non-numeric data into clustering workflows.

entries.trigger: You need a quick linear relationship view.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.regplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `regplot` is the quickest regression check for two numeric variables. It is useful before deeper modeling.
entries.common_bug: Using it on highly nonlinear data and overtrusting the line.

entries.trigger: You want to check model fit errors visually.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.residplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Residual plots help identify nonlinearity and heteroscedasticity. Use them as a model diagnostic, not a final chart.
entries.common_bug: Interpreting a residual plot without checking model assumptions.

entries.trigger: You need bivariate structure with univariate context.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.jointplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip", kind="reg")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `jointplot` is ideal for compact exploratory analysis. It is the fastest way to inspect the relationship plus marginals together.
entries.common_bug: Using a joint plot for very large data without sampling or aggregation.

entries.trigger: You need a matrix of pair plots for a numeric dataset.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.pairplot(df, hue="species", corner=True)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `pairplot` is a fast EDA tool for numeric columns. `corner=True` reduces redundant upper-triangle plots.
entries.common_bug: Running pair plots on too many columns and creating an unreadable grid.

entries.trigger: You need more control than `pairplot` gives.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
g = sns.PairGrid(df, vars=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm"], hue="species")
g.map_diag(sns.histplot)
g.map_offdiag(sns.scatterplot, alpha=0.7)
g.add_legend()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `PairGrid` when each panel needs different plotting logic. It is more flexible than `pairplot`.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to call `add_legend()` after mapping hue.

entries.problem: Build a bivariate plot with marginals.
entries.trigger: You want one focused pair relationship with side distributions.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
g = sns.JointGrid(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
g.plot_joint(sns.scatterplot)
g.plot_marginals(sns.histplot, kde=True)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `JointGrid` gives direct control over the center and marginal axes. Use it when `jointplot` is too rigid.
entries.common_bug: Misplacing plot types on the wrong axes in a custom grid.

entries.problem: Split a scatter plot into facets.
entries.trigger: You want the same chart repeated by category.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.relplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species", col="sex")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `relplot` is the figure-level wrapper for relational plots. Use it when faceting is part of the task.
entries.common_bug: Using axes-level scatter when you really need automatic faceting.

entries.trigger: You need faceted histograms or KDE views.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
sns.displot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", hue="species", col="sex", kind="hist", bins=20)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `displot` is the figure-level entry point for distribution workflows. It is the easiest way to facet distributions.
entries.common_bug: Expecting `displot` to behave like a single Axes plot.

entries.trigger: You need a faceted categorical comparison.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.catplot(data=df, x="day", y="total_bill", hue="sex", col="smoker", kind="box")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `catplot` is the figure-level wrapper for categorical plots. Use it for repeated panels across subsets.
entries.common_bug: Building many manual subplots when `catplot` would be simpler.

entries.trigger: You want one regression panel per subset.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.lmplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="sex", col="smoker")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `lmplot` is the figure-level regression wrapper. It is convenient when subgroup splits matter.
entries.common_bug: Using `regplot` when you need multi-panel regression by group.

entries.trigger: You need row and column conditioning with custom mapping.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
g = sns.FacetGrid(df, row="sex", col="species", margin_titles=True)
g.map_dataframe(sns.scatterplot, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm")
g.add_legend()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `FacetGrid` is the base layout tool for conditional plotting. Use it when you need full control over mapping.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that `map_dataframe` expects column names from the provided DataFrame.

entries.trigger: You want a cleaner publication-style plot.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
ax = sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
sns.despine()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `despine()` is a quick cleanup step after plotting. It works well for many analytical charts.
entries.common_bug: Calling `despine()` before the axes exist.

entries.problem: Move a legend to a better position.
entries.trigger: The legend overlaps data or gets clipped.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
ax = sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species")
sns.move_legend(ax, "upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `move_legend()` when the default legend placement is poor. This is common in faceted and dense plots.
entries.common_bug: Leaving the legend inside the plotting area and obscuring data.

entries.problem: Set titles, labels, ticks, and limits.
entries.trigger: You need final presentation polish.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
ax = sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
ax.set_title("Tip vs Total Bill")
ax.set_xlabel("Total Bill")
ax.set_ylabel("Tip")
ax.set_xlim(0, 60)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use Matplotlib methods on the returned Axes for final polish. This is the standard integration pattern with Seaborn.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to rotate dense tick labels.

entries.trigger: You need to label an important point or region.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
ax = sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
ax.annotate("high bill", xy=(50, 10), xytext=(35, 12), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use annotations sparingly and only for important callouts. They are best for emphasis, not decoration.
entries.common_bug: Placing annotations so they overlap with the data.

entries.trigger: Your data already lives in a DataFrame.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [1.1, 1.9, 3.2, 3.8], "group": ["A", "A", "B", "B"]})
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="x", y="y", hue="group")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Seaborn is optimized for tidy tabular data. This is the most common production workflow.
entries.common_bug: Passing wide data when the function expects long-form columns.

entries.trigger: You have numeric arrays rather than a DataFrame.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(1, 11)
y = np.array([1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.1, 3.6, 4.0, 4.8, 5.3, 5.9, 6.2])
sns.lineplot(x=x, y=y)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: NumPy arrays are fine for quick numeric plots. Add a DataFrame when you need semantic mappings.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that some workflows are easier with named columns.

entries.trigger: You want Seaborn inside a multi-panel Matplotlib figure.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="sex", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Embedded Seaborn Plot")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Passing `ax=` is the standard way to embed Seaborn in custom Matplotlib layouts. It keeps figure orchestration under your control.
entries.common_bug: Assuming Seaborn will create the axes you want when you already own the figure layout.

entries.trigger: You need a PNG or PDF artifact.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
ax = sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("figure.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.savefig("figure.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use PNG for raster output and PDF/SVG for vector graphics. `bbox_inches="tight"` helps prevent clipping.
entries.common_bug: Exporting before tightening layout or moving the legend.

entries.trigger: You need the plot on a colored background or slide deck.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
plt.savefig("transparent.png", dpi=300, transparent=True, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Transparency is useful for slides and compositing. Verify contrast against the target background.
entries.common_bug: Using transparency with low-contrast labels that become unreadable.

entries.problem: Plot a very large dataset efficiently.
entries.trigger: You have millions of rows or heavy overplotting.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("diamonds").dropna()
sample = df.sample(n=min(5000, len(df)), random_state=42)
sns.scatterplot(data=sample, x="carat", y="price", alpha=0.3, linewidth=0)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Sample first when the raw point cloud is too dense. For heavy scatter plots, reduce point size and use transparency.
entries.common_bug: Plotting every row and turning the chart into a dark blob.

entries.problem: Reduce rendering cost for dense layers.
entries.trigger: You need many points but still want a usable plot.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset("diamonds").dropna()
sample = df.sample(n=8000, random_state=42)
ax = sns.scatterplot(data=sample, x="carat", y="price", alpha=0.25, s=10, linewidth=0)
plt.savefig("dense_plot.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Prefer aggregation, sampling, or summary views over raw overplotting. Use vector output carefully for dense point clouds.
entries.common_bug: Repeatedly redrawing the same figure in loops without reuse or caching.

entries.problem: Read or temporarily apply style settings.
entries.trigger: You need to inspect or scope plot style changes without permanently changing the global theme state.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

with sns.axes_style("whitegrid"):
    ax = sns.scatterplot(data=sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna(), x="total_bill", y="tip")
    plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: axes_style() is useful when you want a local style scope. It avoids permanently changing the global theme state.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that theme changes can leak across plots in the same session.

entries.problem: Read or temporarily apply context scaling.
entries.trigger: You need a scoped change to font and line sizing.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

with sns.plotting_context("talk"):
    ax = sns.lineplot(data=sns.load_dataset("flights"), x="year", y="passengers")
    plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use context scaling for figures intended for slides or print. This is cleaner than manual global resizing.
entries.common_bug: Applying large fonts without resizing the figure.

entries.trigger: You need to return to default visual settings.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

sns.reset_defaults()
sns.reset_orig()
entries.minimal_notes: reset_defaults() returns seaborn defaults; reset_orig() restores original Matplotlib settings. Use one intentionally.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to reset after exploratory theme changes.

entries.trigger: You want Seaborn's shorthand colors in Matplotlib plots.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set_theme()
sns.set_color_codes("deep")
plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], color="b")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: This helps align Matplotlib shorthand colors with a Seaborn palette. It is useful when mixing both libraries.
entries.common_bug: Assuming Matplotlib shorthand colors always match your active palette.

entries.problem: Build a custom palette from named colors.
entries.trigger: You need exact control over a categorical palette.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

palette = sns.color_palette(["#4C72B0", "#55A868", "#C44E52", "#8172B2"])
print(palette)
entries.minimal_notes: Use explicit hex values when brand colors matter. This is common in production dashboards.
entries.common_bug: Using too many colors with weak contrast.

entries.problem: Make a diverging palette for centered data.
entries.trigger: You need a palette around a midpoint like zero.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

palette = sns.diverging_palette(220, 20, as_cmap=True)
print(palette)
entries.minimal_notes: Diverging palettes work well for deltas and centered matrices. They are a strong fit for heatmaps and residual views.
entries.common_bug: Using a sequential palette for data that has positive and negative values.

entries.trigger: You need ordered shading for numeric intensity.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

palette = sns.light_palette("seagreen", as_cmap=True)
print(palette)
entries.minimal_notes: Sequential palettes are better when magnitude changes in one direction. Use them for counts, density, and rank-like values.
entries.common_bug: Using dark text over a too-dark sequential palette.

entries.trigger: You want a toned-down or stronger version of one color.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

print(sns.desaturate("steelblue", 0.5))
print(sns.saturate("steelblue"))
entries.minimal_notes: These helpers are useful for making emphasis colors and muted companions. They keep palette harmony better than arbitrary color picks.
entries.common_bug: Tweaking saturation without checking contrast.

entries.problem: Fine-tune a color in HLS space.
entries.trigger: You need a precise lighten/darken adjustment.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

print(sns.set_hls_values("teal", l=0.7, s=0.8))
entries.minimal_notes: This is useful when a palette needs a controlled highlight color. It is more predictable than trial-and-error edits.
entries.common_bug: Changing lightness too far and losing readability.

entries.trigger: You want the modern composable plotting API.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn.objects as so
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
(
    so.Plot(df, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", color="species")
    .add(so.Dot(), so.Jitter(0.2))
)
entries.minimal_notes: The objects interface is good for reusable plot specifications. It is the modern declarative layer in Seaborn 0.13.2.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that the objects interface is separate from axes-level functions.

entries.problem: Build a histogram with the objects API.
entries.trigger: You need explicit control over a binned distribution.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn.objects as so
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
(
    so.Plot(df, x="bill_length_mm")
    .add(so.Bar(), so.Hist())
)
entries.minimal_notes: Hist is the declarative histogram stat in the objects API. It is useful when combining bins with other marks.
entries.common_bug: Mixing up so.Bar() and so.Hist() responsibilities.

entries.trigger: You want a declarative KDE workflow.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn.objects as so
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
(
    so.Plot(df, x="bill_length_mm")
    .add(so.Line(), so.KDE())
)
entries.minimal_notes: KDE gives an explicit density transform in the objects interface. It is useful when you want the same composition model across plot types.
entries.common_bug: Using a density estimate where the sample size is too small for a stable curve.

entries.trigger: You want bars with an explicit estimator workflow.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn.objects as so
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
(
    so.Plot(df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex")
    .add(so.Bar(), so.Est(errorbar="ci"))
)
entries.minimal_notes: Est is the declarative estimator/error-bar stat. It is the objects API equivalent of summary-style categorical plots.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that summary bars show estimates, not raw observations.

entries.trigger: You need a fitted trend in the objects API.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn.objects as so
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
(
    so.Plot(df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
    .add(so.Dot(alpha=0.4))
    .add(so.Line(color="crimson"), so.PolyFit(order=1))
)
entries.minimal_notes: PolyFit is useful for explicit polynomial fitting in the declarative pipeline. It gives a modern alternative to ad hoc trend fitting.
entries.common_bug: Fitting a high-order polynomial and overinterpreting the curve.

entries.problem: Handle dense scatter with positional nudging.
entries.trigger: You need to reduce overlap in crowded point plots.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn.objects as so
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("tips").dropna()
(
    so.Plot(df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex")
    .add(so.Dot(), so.Dodge())
)
entries.minimal_notes: Dodge helps separate overlapping groups along the categorical axis. It is useful for comparative plots with repeated categories.
entries.common_bug: Using dodge when the categories already have no overlap.

entries.trigger: You need to know what demo data can be loaded.
entries.snippet:
import seaborn as sns

print(sns.get_dataset_names())
entries.minimal_notes: This is useful for examples and validation scripts. Treat it as discovery data, not a production catalog.
entries.common_bug: Assuming the dataset list is offline-stable or exhaustive for your use case.

common_errors.cause: NaNs or wrong column names in data, x, or y.
common_errors.solution: Validate column names and drop missing values for the plotted fields.

common_errors.cause: Default legend placement collides with plotted points.
common_errors.solution: Use move_legend() or Matplotlib legend placement.

common_errors.cause: Too many tick labels or dense categories.
common_errors.solution: Rotate ticks, reduce categories, or widen the figure.

common_errors.cause: hue points to the wrong column or to a numeric field unintentionally.
common_errors.solution: Check variable type and intended semantics before plotting.

common_errors.cause: Too many rows or too much overplotting.
common_errors.solution: Sample data, reduce marker size, or use alpha and aggregation.

common_errors.cause: Layout was not tightened before export.

common_errors.error: Plot state changes leak into later figures.
common_errors.cause: Theme settings were applied globally in a shared session.
common_errors.solution: Use context managers or reset seaborn state before the next plot.

common_errors.cause: Default size and context do not match the output medium.
common_errors.solution: Set context, figsize, and export DPI together.

common_errors.cause: Too few points or poor bin/fitting settings.
common_errors.solution: Sample, simplify, or choose a summary view aligned to the data size.

performance_checklist.recommendations: Plot millions of rows with sampling or aggregation first.
Prefer summary plots over raw point clouds when the dataset is dense.
Use alpha, small markers, and linewidth=0 for scatter-heavy charts.
Reuse figures and axes instead of redrawing in loops.
Avoid large pairwise grids unless they answer a real question.
Use rasterization or vector export intentionally based on output density.
Reduce repeated rendering and unnecessary faceting.
Keep memory use low by selecting only the columns needed for the plot.

production_checklist: Palette is accessible and colorblind-safe where needed.
Figure size matches the output medium.
Legend placement does not clip or cover data.
Title and axis labels are present.
Export DPI is appropriate for the target medium.
Results are reproducible with fixed sampling or ordering where needed.
